title: Ackermann Geometry and the Turning Circle: The Bicycle Model, the Two Steering Angles of a Car, the Smallest Circle It Can Drive and the Speed It Can Drive It At

questions.question: Why can a car not turn on the spot?
options: Its steering angle is limited to 24 degrees
The turn rate is the speed times tan(steer) over the wheelbase: no speed, no turn
Its motor drives only the rear wheels
questions.explanation: In the bicycle model the heading changes at the speed times the tangent of the steering angle over the wheelbase. At rest that is zero whatever the steering.

questions.question: The smallest circle of the car was:
questions.explanation: The wheelbase over the tangent of the largest steering angle: 0.3302 over tan 24 degrees.

questions.question: At the smallest circle the inner and the outer front wheels differed by:
options: Nothing: both point the same way
questions.explanation: The inner wheel is on a smaller circle and must be turned more: 27.2 degrees against 21.4.

questions.question: The lane a car needs at its smallest circle is:
questions.explanation: The outer front wheel is ahead of the rear axle and sweeps a larger circle than the car's side. A corridor only as wide as the car cannot be turned in.

questions.question: What sets the fastest speed round a circle on gravel?
questions.explanation: The tyres can give at most the friction times g sideways, so the speed is the root of friction times g times the radius: 1.81 m/s on its smallest circle.

questions.question: Why is the Ackermann difference invisible on a big circle?
options: It only exists at low speed
On a large radius the two angles are nearly equal
The tyres hide it by sliding
questions.explanation: The two front wheels are on circles whose radii differ by the track. On 20 m that is a tenth of a degree; at full lock on a small car, 5.8 degrees.
